claim: Zoonotic spillover from animal reservoirs is responsible for a significant global public health burden.
source: Zoonotic spillover from animal reservoirs is responsible for a significant global public health burden, but the processes that promote spillover events are poorly understood in complex urban settings.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the broader scientific literature on zoonotic diseases.

claim: The processes that promote spillover events are poorly understood in complex urban settings.
source: Zoonotic spillover from animal reservoirs is responsible for a significant global public health burden, but the processes that promote spillover events are poorly understood in complex urban settings.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field and is supported by the literature review in the introduction.

claim: Endemic transmission of Leptospira in marginalised urban communities occurs through human exposure to an environment contaminated by bacteria shed in the urine of the rat reservoir.
source: Endemic transmission of Leptospira, the agent of leptospirosis, in marginalised urban communities occurs through human exposure to an environment contaminated by bacteria shed in the urine of the rat reservoir.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Leptospira transmission mechanisms.

claim: The study was conducted in a high-risk community in Salvador, Brazil.
source: We conducted an eco-epidemiological study in a high-risk community in Salvador, Brazil, by prospectively following a cohort of 1401 residents to ascertain serological evidence for leptospiral infections.
evidence: This is a direct description of the study design and location.

claim: The study prospectively followed a cohort of 1401 residents.
source: We conducted an eco-epidemiological study in a high-risk community in Salvador, Brazil, by prospectively following a cohort of 1401 residents to ascertain serological evidence for leptospiral infections.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study cohort size.

claim: The estimated infection rate was 51.4 (95%CI 40.4, 64.2) infections per 1000 follow-up events.
source: The estimated infection rate was 51.4 (95%CI 40.4, 64.2) infections per 1000 follow-up events.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Infection risk increased with age until 30 years of age.
source: Infection risk increased with age until 30 years of age and was associated with male gender.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of the cohort data.

claim: Infection risk was associated with male gender.
source: Infection risk increased with age until 30 years of age and was associated with male gender.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of the cohort data.

claim: Rattiness was positively associated with infection risk for residents across the entire study area.
source: Rattiness was positively associated with infection risk for residents across the entire study area, but this effect was stronger in higher elevation areas (OR 3.27 95% CI 1.68, 19.07) than in lower elevation areas (OR 1.14 95% CI 1.05, 1.53).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the joint spatial modeling analysis.

claim: The effect of rattiness on infection risk was stronger in higher elevation areas (OR 3.27 95% CI 1.68, 19.07) than in lower elevation areas (OR 1.14 95% CI 1.05, 1.53).
source: Rattiness was positively associated with infection risk for residents across the entire study area, but this effect was stronger in higher elevation areas (OR 3.27 95% CI 1.68, 19.07) than in lower elevation areas (OR 1.14 95% CI 1.05, 1.53).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the joint spatial modeling analysis showing an interaction effect.

claim: Frequent flooding events may disperse bacteria in regions of low elevation.
source: These findings suggest that, while frequent flooding events may disperse bacteria in regions of low elevation, environmental risk in higher elevation areas is more localised and directly driven by the distribution of local rat populations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study findings based on the observed interaction between elevation and rattiness.

claim: Environmental risk in higher elevation areas is more localised and directly driven by the distribution of local rat populations.
source: These findings suggest that, while frequent flooding events may disperse bacteria in regions of low elevation, environmental risk in higher elevation areas is more localised and directly driven by the distribution of local rat populations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study findings based on the observed interaction between elevation and rattiness.

claim: Leptospirosis is estimated to cause more than one million cases globally each year.
source: Globally, it is estimated to cause more than one million cases and over 58,000 deaths each year (Costa et al., 2015a), with an annual global burden of 2.9 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) (Torgerson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Costa et al., 2015a.

claim: Leptospirosis is estimated to cause over 58,000 deaths globally each year.
source: Globally, it is estimated to cause more than one million cases and over 58,000 deaths each year (Costa et al., 2015a), with an annual global burden of 2.9 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) (Torgerson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Costa et al., 2015a.

claim: Leptospirosis has an annual global burden of 2.9 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs).
source: Globally, it is estimated to cause more than one million cases and over 58,000 deaths each year (Costa et al., 2015a), with an annual global burden of 2.9 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) (Torgerson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Torgerson et al., 2015.

claim: The burden of leptospirosis falls heavily on marginalised urban populations in low- and middle-income countries.
source: This burden falls heavily on marginalised urban populations in low- and middle-income countries who live in areas characterised by high population density, poor quality housing and inadequate provision of healthcare, sanitation, and waste management services.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the epidemiology of leptospirosis.

claim: The Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus) is the principal reservoir for leptospiral infection in marginalised urban settings.
source: In these settings, leptospiral infection occurs through contact with water or soil contaminated with leptospires shed in the urine of the principal reservoir, the Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus; Bierque et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bierque et al., 2020.

claim: Leptospires can persist for long periods in the environment.
source: These areas produce the socio-ecological conditions that allow rodent populations to proliferate and leptospires to persist for long periods in the environment (Goarant, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Goarant, 2016.

claim: Socioeconomic vulnerability, household environment and behavioural exposures are important determinants of leptospiral infection risk.
source: Multiple studies have helped to elucidate key aspects of the Leptospira transmission cycle in urban settings, identifying socioeconomic vulnerability, household environment and behavioural exposures as important determinants of infection risk (Reis et al., 2008; Felzemburgh et al., 2014; Hagan et al., 2016; Khalil et al., 2021; Barcellos and Sabroza, 2000; Barcellos and Sabroza, 2001; Mwachui et al., 2015; Keenan et al., 2010; Goarant, 2016; Prabhakaran et al., 2014; Briskin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous studies have been unable to explain fine-scale spatial variation in leptospiral infection risk using socioeconomic and behavioral variables.
source: However, these variables have been unable to explain fine-scale spatial variation in risk (Reis et al., 2008; Hagan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Reis et al., 2008 and Hagan et al., 2016.

claim: There is high spatial and temporal heterogeneity in environmental Leptospira contamination.
source: This is likely to be driven by the high spatial and temporal heterogeneity in environmental risk, observed in recent studies of Leptospira in soil, and surface and sewage waters (Schneider et al., 2018; Casanovas-Massana et al., 2018; Bierque et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Urban Norway rats have been found to have high Leptospira prevalence and shedding rates worldwide.
source: However, urban Norway rats have been found to have high Leptospira prevalence and shedding rates worldwide (Pellizzaro et al., 2019; Costa et al., 2014a; Boey et al., 2019; Yusof et al., 2019; Krøjgaard et al., 2009; Costa et al., 2015b; de Faria et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies from different locations.

claim: Several studies have identified associations between infection risk and household rat sightings and infestation.
source: While several studies have identified associations between infection risk and household rat sightings and infestation (Reis et al., 2008; Costa et al., 2014b; Hagan et al., 2016; Costa et al., 2021; Pellizzaro et al., 2019; Bhardwaj et al., 2008), their ability to explore fine-scale spatial variation in risk was limited by a reliance on household infestation surveys or aggregation of incidence and abundance indices to a common coarse spatial scale.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous studies modeled rat abundance as a regression covariate without accounting for uncertainty in its measurement.
source: All modelled abundance as a regression covariate, thereby not accounting for uncertainty in its measurement.
evidence: This is a critique of previous methodological approaches based on the literature review.

claim: The study was conducted in Pau da Lima community located in Salvador, Northeast Brazil.
source: The study was conducted in Pau da Lima community (13°32'53.47" S; 38°43'51.10" W), a marginalised informal settlement located in the city of Salvador, Northeast Brazil.
evidence: This is a direct description of the study location.

claim: Pau da Lima has a high estimated annual Leptospira infection rate of 35.4 (95% CI, 30.7, 40.6) infections per 1000 annual follow-up events.
source: These factors result in abundant rat populations (Eyre et al., 2020) and a high estimated annual Leptospira infection rate of 35.4 (95% CI, 30.7, 40.6) infections per 1000 annual follow-up events (Hagan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hagan et al., 2016.

claim: Two serosurveys were conducted in August-October 2014 and January-April 2015.
source: We conducted a prospective community cohort study with two serosurveys carried out in August-October 2014 and January-April 2015.
evidence: This is a direct description of the study timeline.

claim: All ground floor households were visited and eligible inhabitants were invited to join the study.
source: After an initial census of the study site, all ground floor households were visited and inhabitants who met the eligibility criteria of ≥5 years of age who had slept ≥3 nights in the previous week in a study household were invited to join the study.
evidence: This is a direct description of the recruitment process.

claim: Eligibility criteria included being ≥5 years of age and having slept ≥3 nights in the previous week in a study household.
source: After an initial census of the study site, all ground floor households were visited and inhabitants who met the eligibility criteria of ≥5 years of age who had slept ≥3 nights in the previous week in a study household were invited to join the study.
evidence: This is a direct description of the eligibility criteria.

claim: Ground floor households are vulnerable to flooding and at high risk for leptospiral transmission.
source: This study focussed on ground floor households because they are vulnerable to flooding and consequently at high risk for leptospiral transmission.
evidence: This is the rationale for focusing on ground floor households.

claim: The microscopic agglutination test (MAT) was used to determine titers of agglutinating antibodies against pathogenic Leptospira.
source: The microscopic agglutination test (MAT) was used to determine titers of agglutinating antibodies against pathogenic Leptospira in sera obtained from the blood samples collected in each serosurvey.
evidence: This is a direct description of the laboratory method used.

claim: Serological samples were reacted with Leptospira interrogans serovars Copenhageni (COPL1) and Cynopteri 3522 C (C3522C).
source: Serological samples were reacted with a panel of two Leptospira reference strains that are dominant in Pau da Lima: Leptospira interrogans serovars Copenhageni (COPL1) and Cynopteri 3522 C (C3522C).
evidence: This is a direct description of the laboratory method.

claim: The two Leptospira strains used have the same performance in identifying MAT seroconversion as the WHO recommended battery of 19 reference serovars.
source: These two strains have been shown to have the same performance in identifying MAT seroconversion in our prospective studies as the WHO recommended battery of 19 reference serovars.
evidence: This is a statement about the validation of the laboratory method used.

claim: Leptospiral infection was defined as seroconversion (an MAT titer increase from negative to ≥1:50) or a fourfold increase in titer for either serovar between paired samples.
source: The study outcome of leptospiral infection was defined as seroconversion, an MAT titer increase from negative to ≥1:50, or a fourfold increase in titer for either serovar between paired samples from cohort subjects.
evidence: This is a direct description of the outcome definition.

claim: The rat ecology study was conducted from October to December 2014.
source: To estimate exposure risk due to local rat contamination between the two serosurveys, a cross-sectional rat ecology study was conducted from October to December 2014.
evidence: This is a direct description of the study timeline.

claim: Data were collected for five indices of rat abundance: live trapping, track plates, number of active burrows present, presence of faecal droppings and presence of trails.
source: Data were collected for five indices of rat abundance: live trapping, track plates, number of active burrows present, presence of faecal droppings and presence of trails.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data collection methods.

claim: Rat trapping was carried out at 189 locations randomly distributed across the study area.
source: Rat trapping was carried out at 189 locations, randomly distributed across the study area (see Panti-May et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a direct description of the sampling design.

claim: Two traps were deployed for 4 consecutive 24 hr trapping periods at each location.
source: Two traps were deployed for 4 consecutive 24 hr trapping periods at each location.
evidence: This is a direct description of the trapping protocol.

claim: Track plates were placed at 415 locations for two consecutive 24 hr periods.
source: Track plates were placed at 415 locations for two consecutive 24 hr periods following the standardised protocol for placement and survey developed and validated previously (Hacker et al., 2016), with five plates placed at each location in the shape of a 'five' on a die.
evidence: This is a direct description of the track plate protocol.

claim: Five track plates were placed at each location in the shape of a 'five' on a die.
source: Track plates were placed at 415 locations for two consecutive 24 hr periods following the standardised protocol for placement and survey developed and validated previously (Hacker et al., 2016), with five plates placed at each location in the shape of a 'five' on a die.
evidence: This is a direct description of the track plate placement protocol.

claim: A survey for signs of rat infestation was conducted within a 10 m radius around each trapping or plate location.
source: On the first day of trapping or plate placement, a survey for signs of rat infestation, adapted from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2006 and validated in the study area (Costa et al., 2014b), was conducted within an area of 10 m radius around each trapping or plate location to record the number of active burrows and the presence of faecal droppings and trails.
evidence: This is a direct description of the survey protocol.

claim: In total, 595 independent locations were sampled for traps, track plates and the three survey indices for signs of rat infestation.
source: In total, 595 independent locations were sampled for traps, track plates and the three survey indices for signs of rat infestation.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the total number of sampling locations.

claim: Three spatially continuous environmental variables were collected: elevation relative to the bottom of each valley, distance to large public refuse piles and the proportion of land cover classified as impervious within a 30 m radius.
source: In addition to the environmental survey conducted at each household location, we also collected information for three spatially continuous environmental variables: elevation relative to the bottom of each valley, distance to large public refuse piles and the proportion of land cover classified as impervious (man-made structures) within a 30 m radius.
evidence: This is a direct description of the environmental data collected.

claim: The land cover variable was created from Digital Globe's WorldView-2 satellite imagery taken on February 17, 2013.
source: The land cover variable was created from Digital Globe's WorldView-2 satellite imagery (8 bands) taken on February 17, 2013 which was classified using a maximum likelihood supervised algorithm and validated with ground truthed data collected from 20 randomly selected sites of size 5 m by 5 m.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data source and processing method.

claim: 3,179 eligible residents were identified using a baseline community census.
source: In Pau da Lima, we identified 3179 eligible residents using a baseline community census, household visits and through other members of the household.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of eligible residents.

claim: 2,018 (63.4%) individuals consented to join the study and provided a blood sample in the first serosurvey.
source: Of these, 2018 (63.4%) individuals consented to join the study and provided a blood sample in the first serosurvey (August-October 2014).
evidence: This is a direct statement about recruitment and participation.

claim: 1,401 (69.4%) participants from 669 households completed the second serosurvey.
source: As a result of loss to follow-up, only 1401 (69.4%) of these participants (from 669 households) completed the second serosurvey (January-April 2015).
evidence: This is a direct statement about follow-up completion.

claim: Individuals lost to follow-up could not be found after at least five attempts (44.4%), had moved out of the study area (31.1%) or did not wish to provide a second blood sample (19.8%).
source: Individuals were lost to follow-up because they could not be found after at least five attempts (44.4%), had moved out of the study area (31.1%) or did not wish to provide a second blood sample (19.8%).
evidence: This is a direct description of reasons for loss to follow-up.

claim: There was serological evidence of 72 leptospiral infections in the cohort between the two serosurveys.
source: Between the two serosurveys there was serological evidence of 72 leptospiral infections in the cohort, with an overall infection rate of 51.4 (95%CI 40.4, 64.2) infections per 1,000 follow-up events.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the primary outcome data.

claim: Valley 2 had an estimated infection rate of 66.4 (95%CI 47.3, 90.2) infections per 1000 follow-up events.
source: Valleys 2 and 3 had high estimated infection rates with 66.4 (95%CI 47.3, 90.2) infections per 1000 follow-up events and 49.6 (95%CI 33.6, 69.9) infections per 1000 follow-up events, respectively, compared to 23.2 (95%CI 9.2, 46.9) infections per 1000 follow-up events in Valley 1.
evidence: This is a direct statement of infection rates by valley.

claim: Valley 3 had an estimated infection rate of 49.6 (95%CI 33.6, 69.9) infections per 1000 follow-up events.
source: Valleys 2 and 3 had high estimated infection rates with 66.4 (95%CI 47.3, 90.2) infections per 1000 follow-up events and 49.6 (95%CI 33.6, 69.9) infections per 1000 follow-up events, respectively, compared to 23.2 (95%CI 9.2, 46.9) infections per 1000 follow-up events in Valley 1.
evidence: This is a direct statement of infection rates by valley.

claim: Valley 1 had an estimated infection rate of 23.2 (95%CI 9.2, 46.9) infections per 1000 follow-up events.
source: Valleys 2 and 3 had high estimated infection rates with 66.4 (95%CI 47.3, 90.2) infections per 1000 follow-up events and 49.6 (95%CI 33.6, 69.9) infections per 1000 follow-up events, respectively, compared to 23.2 (95%CI 9.2, 46.9) infections per 1000 follow-up events in Valley 1.
evidence: This is a direct statement of infection rates by valley.

claim: A rat was captured in 129 (9.0%) out of 1,512 trapping-days.
source: In the rat ecology study a rat was captured in 129 (9.0%) out of 1,512 trapping-days, 263 (37.4%) out of 703 track plate days had at least one positive plate and 28.5%, 19.7%, and 25.9% of the 580 sampled locations had at least one sign of active burrows, faecal droppings and trails, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct statement of rat trapping results.

claim: 263 (37.4%) out of 703 track plate days had at least one positive plate.
source: In the rat ecology study a rat was captured in 129 (9.0%) out of 1,512 trapping-days, 263 (37.4%) out of 703 track plate days had at least one positive plate and 28.5%, 19.7%, and 25.9% of the 580 sampled locations had at least one sign of active burrows, faecal droppings and trails, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct statement of track plate results.

claim: 28.5% of the 580 sampled locations had at least one sign of active burrows.
source: In the rat ecology study a rat was captured in 129 (9.0%) out of 1,512 trapping-days, 263 (37.4%) out of 703 track plate days had at least one positive plate and 28.5%, 19.7%, and 25.9% of the 580 sampled locations had at least one sign of active burrows, faecal droppings and trails, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct statement of survey results.

claim: 19.7% of the 580 sampled locations had at least one sign of faecal droppings.
source: In the rat ecology study a rat was captured in 129 (9.0%) out of 1,512 trapping-days, 263 (37.4%) out of 703 track plate days had at least one positive plate and 28.5%, 19.7%, and 25.9% of the 580 sampled locations had at least one sign of active burrows, faecal droppings and trails, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct statement of survey results.

claim: 25.9% of the 580 sampled locations had at least one sign of trails.
source: In the rat ecology study a rat was captured in 129 (9.0%) out of 1,512 trapping-days, 263 (37.4%) out of 703 track plate days had at least one positive plate and 28.5%, 19.7%, and 25.9% of the 580 sampled locations had at least one sign of active burrows, faecal droppings and trails, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct statement of survey results.

claim: In the lowest elevation areas (0–8 m above the bottom of the valley), relative elevation and rattiness were positively associated with an increase of 0.04 (95%CI 0.00, 0.07) rattiness units per 1 m.
source: In the lowest elevation areas (0–8 m above the bottom of the valley), relative elevation and rattiness were positively associated with an increase of 0.04 (95%CI 0.00, 0.07) rattiness units per 1 m; when interpreting the magnitude of effect estimates note that, by definition, rattiness is defined so as to have variance one.
evidence: This is a finding from the exploratory multivariable analysis.

claim: Rattiness peaked at an elevation of 8 m before declining with increasing elevation by 0.04 (95%CI –0.09, 0.01) units until an elevation of 22 m.
source: Rattiness then peaked at an elevation of 8 m before declining with increasing elevation by 0.04 (95%CI –0.09, 0.01) units until an elevation of 22 m.
evidence: This is a finding from the exploratory multivariable analysis.

claim: Rattiness started to increase again above 22 m elevation by 0.06 (95%CI 0.00, 0.10) units per metre.
source: Rattiness started to increase again above this elevation by 0.06 (95%CI 0.00, 0.10) units per metre.
evidence: This is a finding from the exploratory multivariable analysis.

claim: Rattiness decreased with increasing distance from large refuse piles by 0.07 (95%CI −0.13,–0.01) units per 10 m distance until a distance of 50 m.
source: Rattiness decreased with increasing distance from large refuse piles, a source of food and harbourage, by 0.07 (95%CI −0.13,–0.01) units per 10 m distance until a distance of 50 m, beyond which there was a smaller increase in rattiness of 0.02 (95%CI –0.05, 0.09) per 10 m.
evidence: This is a finding from the exploratory multivariable analysis.

claim: Beyond 50 m from large refuse piles, there was a smaller increase in rattiness of 0.02 (95%CI –0.05, 0.09) per 10 m.
source: Rattiness decreased with increasing distance from large refuse piles, a source of food and harbourage, by 0.07 (95%CI −0.13,–0.01) units per 10 m distance until a distance of 50 m, beyond which there was a smaller increase in rattiness of 0.02 (95%CI –0.05, 0.09) per 10 m.
evidence: This is a finding from the exploratory multivariable analysis.

claim: Impervious land cover was negatively associated with rattiness, decreasing by –0.05 (95%CI −0.08,–0.01) units for every 10% increase in impervious cover.
source: Impervious land cover (defined as the proportion of the area within a 30 m radius around each sampling location classified as pavement or building) was negatively associated with rattiness, decreasing by –0.05 (95%CI −0.08,–0.01) units for every 10% increase in impervious cover.
evidence: This is a finding from the exploratory multivariable analysis.

claim: In the high elevation category area, a unit increase in mean predicted rattiness at the household location was estimated to increase the odds of infection by 6.92 (95%CI 1.88, 25.47).
source: In the high elevation category area, a unit increase in mean predicted rattiness at the household location was estimated to increase the odds of infection by 6.92 (95%CI 1.88, 25.47).
evidence: This is a finding from the exploratory multivariable model.

claim: In the low and medium elevation category areas there was no evidence of a relationship between rattiness and infection risk.
source: In contrast, in the low and medium elevation category areas there was no evidence of a relationship between rattiness and infection risk, as shown in Figure 5.
evidence: This is a finding from the exploratory multivariable model shown in Figure 5.

claim: Infection risk was strongly associated with age, with an individual experiencing an increased odds of infection of 1.09 (95%CI 1.04, 1.19) for every year of life up until 30 years of age.
source: Infection risk was strongly associated with age, with an individual experiencing an increased odds of infection of 1.09 (95%CI 1.04, 1.19) for every year of life up until 30 years of age, and 1.02 (95%CI 0.92, 1.09) for each additional year thereafter.
evidence: This is a finding from the joint rattiness-infection model.

claim: After 30 years of age, the odds of infection increased by 1.02 (95%CI 0.92, 1.09) for each additional year.
source: Infection risk was strongly associated with age, with an individual experiencing an increased odds of infection of 1.09 (95%CI 1.04, 1.19) for every year of life up until 30 years of age, and 1.02 (95%CI 0.92, 1.09) for each additional year thereafter.
evidence: This is a finding from the joint rattiness-infection model.

claim: Male participants were more likely to be infected than female participants (OR 2.69 95% CI 1.58, 5.89).
source: Male participants were more likely to be infected than female participants (OR 2.69 95% CI 1.58, 5.89).
evidence: This is a finding from the joint rattiness-infection model.

claim: Individuals living in Valley 2 had a higher estimated odds of infection (OR 2.91 95% CI 1.03, 20.82) compared with individuals living in Valley 1.
source: Compared with individuals living in Valley 1, those living in Valley 2 had a higher estimated odds of infection (OR 2.91 95% CI 1.03, 20.82).
evidence: This is a finding from the joint rattiness-infection model.

claim: Individuals living in the medium elevation areas had a lower estimated odds of infection (OR 0.77 95% CI 0.31, 1.66) relative to those living in the low relative elevation category area.
source: Individuals living in the medium (OR 0.77 95% CI 0.31, 1.66) and high (OR 0.67 95% CI 0.11, 1.64) elevation areas had a lower estimated odds of infection relative to those living in the low relative elevation category area where there are open sewers and flooding risk is higher, however these confidence intervals included an odds ratio of one (not statistically significant at the conventional 5% level).
evidence: This is a finding from the joint rattiness-infection model.

claim: Individuals living in the high elevation areas had a lower estimated odds of infection (OR 0.67 95% CI 0.11, 1.64) relative to those living in the low relative elevation category area.
source: Individuals living in the medium (OR 0.77 95% CI 0.31, 1.66) and high (OR 0.67 95% CI 0.11, 1.64) elevation areas had a lower estimated odds of infection relative to those living in the low relative elevation category area where there are open sewers and flooding risk is higher, however these confidence intervals included an odds ratio of one (not statistically significant at the conventional 5% level).
evidence: This is a finding from the joint rattiness-infection model.

claim: Infection risk was positively associated with rattiness for households situated in all three levels of the relative elevation category variable.
source: Infection risk was positively associated with rattiness for households situated in all three levels of the relative elevation category variable.
evidence: This is a finding from the joint rattiness-infection model.

claim: In the low elevation area, the effect of rattiness on infection risk was OR 1.14 95% CI 1.05, 1.53 per unit increase in rattiness.
source: However, while the effect size (per unit increase in rattiness) was similar in the low (OR 1.14 95% CI 1.05, 1.53) and medium (OR 1.25 95% CI 1.08, 1.74) elevation areas, in the high elevation area the effect of increasing rattiness on infection risk was significantly stronger (OR 3.27 95% CI 1.68, 19.07).
evidence: This is a finding from the joint rattiness-infection model.

claim: In the medium elevation area, the effect of rattiness on infection risk was OR 1.25 95% CI 1.08, 1.74 per unit increase in rattiness.
source: However, while the effect size (per unit increase in rattiness) was similar in the low (OR 1.14 95% CI 1.05, 1.53) and medium (OR 1.25 95% CI 1.08, 1.74) elevation areas, in the high elevation area the effect of increasing rattiness on infection risk was significantly stronger (OR 3.27 95% CI 1.68, 19.07).
evidence: This is a finding from the joint rattiness-infection model.

claim: In the high elevation area, the effect of rattiness on infection risk was OR 3.27 95% CI 1.68, 19.07 per unit increase in rattiness.
source: However, while the effect size (per unit increase in rattiness) was similar in the low (OR 1.14 95% CI 1.05, 1.53) and medium (OR 1.25 95% CI 1.08, 1.74) elevation areas, in the high elevation area the effect of increasing rattiness on infection risk was significantly stronger (OR 3.27 95% CI 1.68, 19.07).
evidence: This is a finding from the joint rattiness-infection model.

claim: There was heterogeneous spatial variation in predicted rattiness.
source: There was heterogeneous spatial variation in predicted rattiness.
evidence: This is a description of the prediction results shown in Figure 6.

claim: The low elevation areas in the central length of each valley had high mean predicted rattiness.
source: The low elevation areas in the central length of each valley (relative elevation is shown in Figure 6 - panel E with the contours marking the low, medium and high elevation areas) had high mean predicted rattiness.
evidence: This is a description of the prediction results shown in Figure 6.

claim: High rattiness was predicted in several high elevation areas, including the northern tip of Valley 3 and several small hotspots along the three valley's high elevation sides.
source: High rattiness was also predicted in several high elevation areas, for example the northern tip of Valley 3 and several small hotspots along the three valley's high elevation sides.
evidence: This is a description of the prediction results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Infection risk was low across most of Valley 1 (<2.5%).
source: Infection risk was low across most of Valley 1 (<2.5%), with marginally higher average values found in the central low elevation area (2.5–5%).
evidence: This is a description of the prediction results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Risk was consistently higher across most of Valleys 2 and 3 (7.5–15%).
source: Risk was consistently higher across most of Valleys 2 and 3 (7.5–15%), with the effect of elevation on risk clearly visible.
evidence: This is a description of the prediction results shown in Figure 6.

claim: In areas with higher and more spatially heterogeneous predicted infection risk, this was driven by high levels of predicted rattiness.
source: In areas with higher and more spatially heterogeneous predicted infection risk, for example in the central region of Valley 2, this was driven by high levels of predicted rattiness.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the prediction results shown in Figure 6.

claim: The finding that rattiness was associated with infection risk indicates that the spatial distribution of rat populations was an important driver of transmission close to the household across the entire study area.
source: The finding that rattiness was associated with infection risk indicates that the spatial distribution of rat populations was an important driver of transmission close to the household across the entire study area.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study findings.

claim: There was no residual spatial correlation in the infection data after accounting for rattiness.
source: There was no residual spatial correlation in the infection data after accounting for rattiness in our analysis, possibly suggesting that previously unexplained spatial heterogeneity in risk could be driven by variation in rattiness (Hagan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the model fitting process.

claim: Previously unexplained spatial heterogeneity in risk could be driven by variation in rattiness.
source: There was no residual spatial correlation in the infection data after accounting for rattiness in our analysis, possibly suggesting that previously unexplained spatial heterogeneity in risk could be driven by variation in rattiness (Hagan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings in relation to previous work.

claim: The model predicted high average rattiness across the low elevation areas where leptospiral transmission is high.
source: Our model also predicted high average rattiness across the low elevation areas where leptospiral transmission is high (Hagan et al., 2016; Reis et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a description of the prediction results in relation to previous findings.

claim: Abundant rat populations are responsible for high levels of observed environmental contamination across lower elevation areas.
source: This supports the hypothesis that abundant rat populations are responsible for high levels of observed environmental contamination across these lower areas (Casanovas-Massana et al., 2018; Casanovas-Massana et al., 2022), and consequently increased infection risk.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The weaker effect of rattiness on infection risk at low and medium elevation areas relative to high elevation areas may be explained by differences in their hydrological profiles.
source: The weaker effect of rattiness on infection risk at low and medium elevation areas relative to high elevation areas may be explained by differences in their hydrological profiles.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the interaction effect.

claim: Low and medium elevation areas are prone to high levels of water runoff and flooding which disperses the pathogen across these areas.
source: While high rat abundance in low and medium areas results in high leptospiral contamination, these areas are prone to high levels of water runoff and flooding. This disperses the pathogen across low elevation areas.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation for the observed interaction effect based on knowledge of the study area.

claim: Leptospires can persist in the environment for weeks or months.
source: The ability of leptospires to persist in the environment for weeks or months means that this process can significantly increase environmental risk in low elevation areas for long periods.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Leptospira ecology.

claim: Water dispersal of leptospires disconnects shedding and infection events in space and time.
source: This process disconnects shedding and infection events in space and time (Plowright et al., 2017) and obscures the relationship between infection risk and rattiness in low and medium elevation households.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mechanism supported by a citation to Plowright et al., 2017.

claim: High elevation areas have lower levels of water runoff and flooding due to improved drainage and sewage systems, and a smaller upstream catchment area for rainfall.
source: In contrast, high elevation areas have lower levels of water runoff and flooding due to improved drainage and sewage systems, and a smaller upstream catchment area for rainfall.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the study area and general hydrological principles.

claim: In high elevation areas, leptospires are less likely to be washed away from the location at which they were shed, and environmental risk remains more localised and strongly associated with the spatial distribution of rats.
source: Leptospires are consequently less likely to be washed away from the location at which they were shed, and environmental risk remains more localised and strongly associated with the spatial distribution of rats.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mechanism explaining the interaction effect.

claim: The hypothesised role of hydrology in the aggregation and dispersal of leptospires is supported by a recent study in low elevation areas of Pau da Lima which found that soil contamination was not associated with local rat activity.
source: This hypothesised role of hydrology in the aggregation and dispersal of leptospires (Plowright et al., 2017) is supported by a recent study in low elevation areas of Pau da Lima which found that soil contamination was not associated with local rat activity (Schneider et al., 2018).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by a citation to Schneider et al., 2018.

claim: The finding that rattiness was associated with infection in low and medium elevation areas suggests that the spatial distribution of environmental risk in these areas is not entirely determined by water dispersal.
source: However, our finding that rattiness was associated with infection in low and medium elevation areas suggests that the spatial distribution of environmental risk in these areas is not entirely determined by water dispersal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study findings.

claim: A previous study found that the probability of a surface water sample being positive for Leptospira was highest in low elevation areas and lowest in medium elevation areas, with no significant difference between low and high elevation areas.
source: Interestingly, a previous study of surface waters in Pau da Lima found that the probability of a sample being positive for Leptospira was highest in low elevation areas and lowest in medium elevation areas, with no significant difference between low and high elevation areas (Casanovas-Massana et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Casanovas-Massana et al., 2018.

claim: The pattern of Leptospira contamination in surface waters is consistent with the study's findings and suggests there may be a 'washing out' of locally deposited leptospires in medium elevation areas but not in high elevation areas.
source: This is consistent with our findings and suggests that there may be a 'washing out' of locally deposited leptospires in medium elevation areas but not in high elevation areas.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the current findings with previous work.

claim: Improving drainage systems at all elevation levels can reduce the dispersal of leptospires from high to low elevation areas.
source: Improving drainage systems at all elevation levels can reduce the dispersal of leptospires from high to low elevation areas.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: Closure of sewer systems can protect local residents from exposure and reduce the introduction of additional contamination from upstream sewer water.
source: Closure of sewer systems, which generally run through low elevation areas, can protect local residents from exposure and reduce the introduction of additional contamination from upstream sewer water.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: Paving over soil surfaces can reduce the surface area over which leptospires can persist, reducing environmental risk.
source: Paving over soil surfaces can reduce the surface area over which leptospires can persist (Bierque et al., 2020), reducing environmental risk further.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study findings and supported by a citation.

claim: A reduction in the dispersal and accumulation of bacteria will result in more localised environmental risk.
source: A reduction in the dispersal and accumulation of bacteria will result in more localised environmental risk, as was observed in the high elevation areas in this study.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the study findings.

claim: Reduced environmental exposure for rats may lower shedding rates and act as a feedback loop into the Leptospira transmission cycle.
source: This may also reduce environmental exposure for rats, thereby lowering shedding rates and acting as a feedback loop into the Leptospira transmission cycle (Minter et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by a citation to Minter et al., 2018.

claim: Chemical rodenticide campaigns have limited and short-term impact on Norway rat abundance in marginalised urban settings.
source: Given the limited and short-term impact of chemical rodenticide campaigns on Norway rat abundance in these settings (de Masi et al., 2009), longer-term environment management strategies targeted at rattiness hotspots may also be needed to reduce the availability of key predictors of rattiness, such as large refuse piles and vegetation and soil land cover.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to de Masi et al., 2009.

claim: The study was designed to explore the spatial variation in rattiness and infection risk in Pau da Lima during the driest period of the year.
source: Our study was designed to explore the spatial variation in rattiness and infection risk in Pau da Lima during the driest period of the year, and it may not be representative of transmission mechanisms during the rainy season.
evidence: This is a statement about the study design and its limitations.

claim: Two recent studies in Pau da Lima reported low seasonal variation in both rat abundance and spatial infection risk patterns.
source: There is some evidence, however, that this may not necessarily be the case, with two recent studies in Pau da Lima reporting low seasonal variation in both rat abundance (Panti-May et al., 2016) and spatial infection risk patterns (Hagan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Panti-May et al., 2016 and Hagan et al., 2016.

claim: The study used household location to link rattiness to an individual, under the assumption that the majority of their exposure occurs close to home.
source: In this study we used household location to link rattiness to an individual, under the assumption that the majority of their exposure occurs close to home.
evidence: This is a statement about a methodological assumption.

claim: 80% of rats are estimated to be actively shedding Leptospira in Pau da Lima.
source: Given that 80% of rats are estimated to be actively shedding Leptospira in Pau da Lima (Costa et al., 2015b; de Faria et al., 2008) and prevalence in rats is generally high in urban areas globally (Pellizzaro et al., 2019; Costa et al., 2014a; Boey et al., 2019; Yusof et al., 2019; Krøjgaard et al., 2009), the use of rattiness as a proxy for rat shedding appears reasonable and it may be a useful proxy in other epidemiological studies.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Costa et al., 2015b and de Faria et al., 2008.

claim: The use of rattiness as a proxy for rat shedding appears reasonable and may be useful in other epidemiological studies.
source: Given that 80% of rats are estimated to be actively shedding Leptospira in Pau da Lima (Costa et al., 2015b; de Faria et al., 2008) and prevalence in rats is generally high in urban areas globally (Pellizzaro et al., 2019; Costa et al., 2014a; Boey et al., 2019; Yusof et al., 2019; Krøjgaard et al., 2009), the use of rattiness as a proxy for rat shedding appears reasonable and it may be a useful proxy in other epidemiological studies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high shedding rates observed.

claim: The rattiness-infection modelling framework is a flexible tool for exploring the spatial association between reservoir abundance, the environment and human health outcomes.
source: The rattiness-infection modelling framework is a flexible tool for exploring the spatial association between reservoir abundance, the environment and human health outcomes.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: The framework provides a statistically principled method for joint spatial modelling of infection risk and multiple indices of reservoir abundance.
source: It provides a statistically principled method for joint spatial modelling of infection risk and multiple indices of reservoir abundance, pooling data between indices and directly accounting for uncertainty in their measurement in all parameter estimates and predictions.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach.

claim: The framework's geostatistical structure enables mapping of both infection risk and rattiness.
source: The framework's geostatistical structure includes spatially continuous predictors for abundance and accounts for spatial correlation, enabling mapping of both infection risk and rattiness.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach.

claim: One limitation of the framework is its dependence on the availability of spatially continuous environmental variables and abundance data, both of which are prone to high measurement error.
source: One inherent limitation is its dependence on the availability of spatially continuous environmental variables and abundance data, both of which are prone to high measurement error.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the methodological approach.

claim: High measurement error in environmental and abundance data can result in high uncertainty in the model parameter estimates and predictions.
source: This can result in high uncertainty in the model parameter estimates and predictions, as demonstrated by the wider confidence intervals for risk factors in the joint model compared to the standard mixed-effects logistic regression analysis.
evidence: This is an observation about the model results.

claim: The framework may have important applications beyond the study of zoonotic spillover, with the rattiness component replaced by other exposure measures such as mosquito density or ecological indices.
source: The framework may have important applications beyond the study of zoonotic spillover, with the rattiness component replaced by other exposure measures for example mosquito density or ecological indices (such as pollution, where there are multiple, related measures of air or groundwater quality) to model associations with human or animal health outcomes.
evidence: This is a statement about potential future applications of the framework.

claim: This is the first study to jointly model rodent abundance and human infection data for a rodent-borne zoonosis.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first study to jointly model rodent abundance and human infection data for a rodent-borne zoonosis.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the methodological approach.

claim: The findings provide new insights into how the dominant mechanisms of Leptospira transmission within complex urban settings may vary over small distances.
source: The findings provide new insights into how the dominant mechanisms of Leptospira transmission within complex urban settings may vary over small distances, as a result of interactions between rats, the environment, geography, and local epidemiology.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the contribution of the study.

claim: The extent to which local rat shedding drives spillover transmission is moderated by elevation, most likely a proxy for water runoff.
source: We demonstrate its potential by applying it to Leptospira in an urban setting, finding evidence that the extent to which local rat shedding drives spillover transmission is moderated by elevation, most likely a proxy for water runoff.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding and its interpretation.
